message.content:
# Target
The compiled C++ binary is /workspace/dataset/test5_executable .
Its source (the test driver only) is /workspace/dataset/test5.cpp :

    if (argc < 2) return 1;
    std::string url = argv[1];
    url_parser::URL parser(url);
    std::cout << parser.scheme() << std::endl;   // line 1
    std::cout << parser.host()   << std::endl;   // line 2
    std::cout << parser.port()   << std::endl;   // line 3  (an integer; -1 when absent)
    std::cout << parser.path()   << std::endl;   // line 4
    std::cout << parser.query()  << std::endl;   // line 5

So EVERY successful run prints exactly 5 newline-terminated lines. Empty fields print as empty lines.
The library source is NOT available and you must NOT try to find or read it. Pure black-box probing.

# How to probe (IMPORTANT)
Run it like:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'THE_URL'
To see exact bytes including empty trailing lines, ALWAYS capture with a delimiter, e.g.:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | sed -n 'l' ; echo "exit=${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
or the most reliable formatting for reporting — number every line:
    /workspace/dataset/test5_executable 'http://a.com' | cat -A | nl -ba
Use single quotes around the URL. For URLs containing single quotes, control characters, or
non-UTF8 bytes, use perl to exec with an exact argv, e.g.:
    perl -e 'exec("/workspace/dataset/test5_executable", "http://a\x27b.com")' | cat -A | nl -ba
Batch many probes in ONE bash call with a loop so you use few tool calls, e.g.:
    for u in 'http://a' 'http://a:1' 'a://b'; do printf '=== [%s]\n' "$u"; /workspace/dataset/test5_executable "$u" | cat -A | nl -ba; done
`cat -A` renders end-of-line as `$`, tabs as `^I`, so an empty field shows as a line containing only `$`.
Probe generously — dozens to hundreds of inputs. It is cheap. Note python3 is NOT installed; perl is.
Do not write anything into /workspace/dataset or /output. Use /tmp for scratch files.

# What to report
Report the OBSERVED FACTS, not guesses. For each rule you state, cite at least one concrete
input and its exact 5 field values. If two plausible rules both explain your data, say so and
design a discriminating probe, then run it. Be exhaustive within your assigned dimension.


Dimension: PORT parsing. port() returns an integer printed via std::cout.
Determine exactly how the port substring is located and converted to an int.
Probe at minimum: 'http://a.com' (expect -1), 'http://a.com:8080', 'http://a.com:80',
'http://a.com:0', 'http://a.com:00080' (leading zeros -> 80?), 'http://a.com:' (empty port),
'http://a.com:/p', 'http://a.com:abc', 'http://a.com:80abc', 'http://a.com:abc80',
'http://a.com:8 0', 'http://a.com:+80', 'http://a.com:-80', 'http://a.com: 80', 'http://a.com:80 ',
'http://a.com:65535', 'http://a.com:65536', 'http://a.com:99999', 'http://a.com:2147483647',
'http://a.com:2147483648' (int overflow? does it throw/abort/clamp?), 'http://a.com:4294967296',
'http://a.com:99999999999999999999', 'http://a.com:0x50', 'http://a.com:080',
'http://a.com:8080:9090', 'http://a:1:2/p', 'http://a.com:8080/p:q', 'http://a.com/p:80',
'http://a.com?x=:80', 'http://user:pass@a.com' (is 'pass' read as a port?),
'http://user:pass@a.com:8080', 'http://a.com:8080?q=1', 'http://a.com:8080#f'.
CRITICAL: for any input that makes the program crash, abort, or throw (non-zero exit / stderr
output), record the exact exit code and the exact stderr text — capture with
`prog 'url' > /tmp/o 2>/tmp/e; echo "exit=$?"; cat -A /tmp/o; echo "--stderr--"; cat /tmp/e`.
Report whether -1 means "no colon found" vs "empty/invalid port". Nail down the exact numeric
conversion semantics (std::stoi-like prefix parse? atoi? full-string check?).

- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text: I have comprehensive data. Let me record the findings.

input.dimension: PORT parsing — how the port substring is located within the URL and how it is converted to the int returned by port()

rules.rule: No input crashes, aborts, or lets an exception escape. Across ~200 probes (including a 100000-digit port, a 100000-zero port, 5000 leading spaces, and all 256 possible single leading bytes) the program always exited 0, wrote nothing to stderr, and printed exactly 5 newline-terminated lines.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com:' + 100000 '9' chars -> exit=0, stderr empty, lines: http / a.com / -1 / '' / ''. Byte-scan of 'http://a.com:<BYTE>80' for BYTE=1..255 -> every case exit=0, sig=0, stderr empty.

rules.rule: A port is only ever looked for inside an authority, and an authority only exists when the URL contains '//' immediately after the scheme's ':'. With no '://' the whole string becomes the path and port is -1.
The authority ends at the first '/', '?', or '#' after the '//'. A ':' at or after that point is never treated as a port separator.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com/p:80' -> http/a.com/-1//p:80/''. 'http://a.com?x=:80' -> http/a.com/-1/''/x=:80. 'http://a.com#f:80' -> http/a.com/-1/''/''. Contrast 'http://a.com:80/:90' -> http/a.com/80//:90/'' and 'http://a.com:8080/p/:9090' -> 8080 with path /p/:9090.

rules.rule: Userinfo is stripped from the authority BEFORE the port colon is located, and the split is at the FIRST '@' in the authority (not the last). So a ':' that lies inside the userinfo is never read as a port.
rules.evidence: 'http://user:80@a.com' -> http/a.com/-1/''/'' (the '80' is NOT taken as a port). 'http://u:1@v:2@a.com:3' -> http/v/2/''/'' — first-'@' stripping leaves 'v:2@a.com:3', giving host 'v' and port-string '2@a.com:3' -> 2. Last-'@' stripping would have given host a.com and port 3. Also 'http://u@a.com:80@b.com:90' -> http/a.com/80/''/'' and 'http://a.com:80@b.com:90/p' -> http/b.com/90//p/''.

rules.rule: Inside the remaining host-part, the port string is taken from immediately after the FIRST ':' (later colons are not special to the splitter). Host is everything before that first colon.
rules.evidence: 'http://[::1]:8080' -> http/'['/-1/''/'' — host is the single char '[', proving the split is at the first ':' and the port-string was '::1]:8080' (unparseable). 'https://[2001:db8::1]:443' -> https/'[2001'/-1/''/''. 'http://a.com::8080' -> http/a.com/-1/''/''. 'http://a.com:8080:9090' -> http/a.com/8080/''/''. 'http://a.com:80:' -> 80.

rules.rule: Conversion is a std::stoi-style base-10 PREFIX parse of the port string, not a full-string validation: optional run of leading whitespace, then an optional single '+' or '-', then ASCII decimal digits; parsing stops at the first non-digit and all trailing bytes are silently ignored.
rules.evidence: Trailing junk ignored: 'http://a.com:80abc' -> 80; 'http://a.com:0080abc' -> 80; 'http://a.com:80.5' -> 80; 'http://a.com:1e3' -> 1; 'http://a.com:8 0' -> 8; 'http://a.com:8_0' -> 8; 'http://a.com:1;2' -> 1; 'http://a.com:80%20' -> 80; 'http://a.com:80 ' -> 80. Leading whitespace accepted: 'http://a.com: 80' -> 80; 'http://a.com:  80' -> 80; 'http://a.com:\t80' -> 80. Leading sign accepted: 'http://a.com:+80' -> 80; 'http://a.com: +80' -> 80; 'http://a.com:-0' -> 0. Order enforced (space cannot follow sign): 'http://a.com:+ 80' -> -1; 'http://a.com:- 80' -> -1; 'http://a.com:++80' -> -1; 'http://a.com:-+80' -> -1. No leading digit at all -> -1: 'http://a.com:abc' -> -1; 'http://a.com:abc80' -> -1; 'http://a.com:.80' -> -1; 'http://a.com:%2280' -> -1.

rules.rule: The radix is fixed at 10. Leading zeros are NOT octal and '0x'/'0X' is NOT hex — the parse just consumes decimal digits.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com:080' -> 80 (octal would be 64); 'http://a.com:0777' -> 777 (octal would be 511); 'http://a.com:00080' -> 80; 'http://a.com:0x50' -> 0 (hex would be 80); 'http://a.com:0X50' -> 0; 'http://a.com:0b11' -> 0.

rules.rule: The accepted leading-whitespace set is exactly C-locale isspace: 0x09 TAB, 0x0A LF, 0x0B VT, 0x0C FF, 0x0D CR, 0x20 SPACE. Every other non-digit, non-'+' leading byte yields -1.
rules.evidence: Exhaustive byte scan of 'http://a.com:<BYTE>80' for BYTE=1..255: the only bytes producing a non-(-1) port were 9,10,11,12,13,32 (all -> 80), 43 '+' (-> 80), and 48-57 (digits, '0'->80, '1'->180, ... '9'->980). Byte 45 '-' produced -1. Byte 0xFF produced -1.

rules.rule: Only ASCII digits count; no Unicode digit forms are recognized.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com:٨٠' (UTF-8 bytes d9 a8 d9 a0, Arabic-Indic 80) -> http/a.com/-1/''/''. 'http://a.com:１２３' (fullwidth 123) -> http/a.com/-1/''/''.

rules.rule: After conversion there is an explicit range check: the value is accepted only if 0 <= v <= 65535; anything else returns -1. There is NO clamping, NO wrapping, and NO 16-bit truncation.
rules.evidence: Boundary: 'http://a.com:65535' -> 65535, 'http://a.com:65534' -> 65534, 'http://a.com:+65535' -> 65535, 'http://a.com:00065535' -> 65535; 'http://a.com:65536' -> -1, 'http://a.com:00065536' -> -1, 'http://a.com:+65536' -> -1, 'http://a.com:655360' -> -1, 'http://a.com:99999' -> -1. Zero accepted: 'http://a.com:0' -> 0, 'http://a.com:+0' -> 0, 'http://a.com:-0' -> 0, 'http://a.com:  +0  ' -> 0, 100000 zeros -> 0. Negatives rejected: 'http://a.com:-1' -> -1, 'http://a.com:-80' -> -1, 'http://a.com:-65535' -> -1. Rules out uint16_t storage (65536 would print 0). Rules out a bare (int) cast of a long strtol result with no range check: 'http://a.com:4294967296' -> -1, not 0. Rules out any clamping: 'http://a.com:2147483647x' -> -1, not 65535 and not 2147483647.

rules.rule: An out-of-int-range numeric prefix is caught and also yields -1 (i.e. the throwing/erroring conversion is wrapped, and its failure is mapped to the same sentinel).
The conversion is NOT atoi/strtol-without-failure-detection: a 'no conversion performed' condition is detected and distinguished from a parsed 0.
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com:abc' -> -1, whereas atoi("abc") == 0 would have printed 0. Compare 'http://a.com:0x50' -> 0 (a real parsed zero). Likewise 'http://a.com:' (empty) -> -1 and 'http://a.com: ' (whitespace only) -> -1.

rules.rule: -1 is a single overloaded sentinel meaning 'no usable port'. It is emitted for all of: no ':' in the authority, an empty port string, a whitespace-only port string, a port string with no leading digits, and a numerically out-of-range port. These cases are NOT distinguishable from port() alone. Because the valid range is 0..65535, -1 can never be a genuine port value.
rules.evidence: no colon: 'http://a.com' -> -1. empty: 'http://a.com:' -> -1 and 'http://a.com:/p' -> http/a.com/-1//p/''. whitespace-only: 'http://a.com: ' -> -1. non-numeric: 'http://a.com:abc' -> -1. out of range: 'http://a.com:65536' -> -1. negative: 'http://a.com:-80' -> -1.

rules.rule: An invalid or out-of-range port does not abort or poison the rest of the parse: the host is still truncated at the colon, and path/query are still extracted normally.
There is no length limit or sanity cap on the port string; the numeric value alone decides. Arbitrarily long leading-zero runs parse fine.
An empty host does not prevent port parsing; the port colon can be the very first character of the authority.
Spaces inside the authority do not terminate it, so a space between host and ':' still yields a parsed port (with the space kept in host).
rules.evidence: 'http://a.com :80' -> http/'a.com '/80/''/''. Also ' http://a.com:80' -> ' http'/a.com/80/''/'' — no trimming of the input at all.

rules.rule: A NUL byte in argv simply truncates the URL at the C-string level before the library sees it; this is not port logic.
rules.evidence: argv 'http://a.com:80\x0090' -> http/a.com/80/''/'' (behaves as 'http://a.com:80'). argv 'http://a.com:\x0080' -> http/a.com/-1/''/'' (behaves as 'http://a.com:').

rules.rule: For every valid in-range numeric port the returned value equals the decimal value exactly (identity mapping, no off-by-one, no reserved-port special-casing).

uncertainties: Whether the port substring handed to the converter is 'everything after the first colon to the end of the host-part' or 'the text between the first and second colon'. These two hypotheses are observationally EQUIVALENT for every probe I could design, because ':' is never a digit and therefore always terminates the prefix parse at exactly the same place. Discriminating probes attempted and found non-discriminating: 'http://a.com:8080:9090' (8080 either way), 'http://a.com:65536:80' / 'http://a.com: :80' / 'http://a.com:+:80' (-1 either way), 'http://a.com:/80' (-1 either way). The 'host = text before first colon' half IS nailed down by 'http://[::1]:8080' -> host '['.

Whether the converter is std::stoi wrapped in try/catch, or strtol/strtoul with an endptr!=start and ERANGE check. Both explain 100% of the data. Definitively RULED OUT: (a) atoi / no-failure-detection, since 'http://a.com:abc' -> -1 not 0; (b) std::from_chars or a hand-rolled isdigit loop, since ' 80' and '+80' both parse; (c) storage in uint16_t, since ':65536' -> -1 not 0; (d) an unchecked (int) narrowing of a long result, since ':4294967296' -> -1 not 0.

Whether the range test is signed ('v < 0 || v > 65535' on an int) or unsigned ('v > 65535' after an unsigned parse). ':-0' -> 0 proves the '-' character is consumed by the converter rather than rejected as a bad char, but every other negative magnitude (-1, -80, -65535, -2147483648) yields -1 under either formulation. A signed int parse plus a two-sided range check is the simplest fit and matches the -1 sentinel being an int.

Whether the -1 for 'no colon present' and the -1 for 'colon present but unparseable/out-of-range' come from the same code path or from two different assignments. port() alone cannot distinguish them; no other printed field changes (host is truncated at the colon in both the valid and invalid cases, e.g. 'http://a.com:abc' -> host 'a.com').

Whether leading-whitespace skipping and '+' acceptance are deliberate or merely inherited defaults of the underlying conversion function. Behaviorally they are present; intent is unknowable black-box.

Behavior under a non-C locale was not exercised (the process ran with the default environment). If the implementation uses a locale-sensitive conversion, digit/whitespace classification could in principle differ elsewhere.
Whether port() is recomputed per call or cached at construction — the driver calls it once, so this is unobservable.
